From `core_manager_find_closest_screen_fallback_call_frequency_test.py`, the test builds `queries` with nested loops over `gx in range(-180, 980, 140)` and `gy in range(-140, 920, 160)`, filtering by the condition on line 32, then transforming each accepted point with the formulas on lines 33–34. The test later asserts `len(queries) == 47`, so `probe.find_closest_screen(x, y)` is executed 47 times in the loop after the additional per-index adjustments on lines 47–50.

From `libqtile/core/manager.py`, `find_closest_screen` first calls `find_screen`. If exactly one screen contains the point, it returns immediately. Otherwise it builds `x_match` and `y_match` by checking whether the point lies in each screen’s horizontal band or vertical band. It returns directly if `len(x_match) == 1` or `len(y_match) == 1`. Only when neither of those single-match cases applies does it call `self._find_closest_closest(x, y, x_match + y_match)` on line 796.

So the quantity asked for is: among the 47 transformed query points, how many produce:
- no exact containing screen from `find_screen`, and
- not exactly one `x_match`, and
- not exactly one `y_match`.

- A: x 0..360, y 0..300
- B: x 220..640, y 40..380
- C: x 80..460, y 240..600
- D: x 460..880, y 220..580
- E: x 700..960, y -60..200

The fallback helper `_find_closest_closest` itself does not recurse or trigger additional calls to the same function; it just filters candidates and picks the nearest center. Therefore the total call count is exactly the number of loop iterations whose coordinates reach line 796 in `find_closest_screen`.
